In [[mathematics]], a '''quasi-analytic''' class of '''functions''' is a generalization of the class of real [[analytic function]]s based upon the following fact: If ''f'' is an analytic function on an interval [''a'',''b'']&nbsp;&sub;&nbsp;'''R''', and at some point ''f'' and all of its derivatives are zero, then ''f'' is identically zero on all of [''a'',''b'']. Quasi-analytic classes are broader classes of functions for which this statement still holds true.

== Definitions ==

Let <math>M=\{M_k\}_{k=0}^\infty</math> be a sequence of [[positive real numbers]]. Then the Denjoy–Carleman class of functions ''C''<sup>''M''</sup>([''a'',''b'']) is defined to be those ''f''&nbsp;&isin;&nbsp;''C''<sup>&infin;</sup>([''a'',''b'']) which satisfy
: <math>\left |\frac{d^kf}{dx^k}(x) \right | \leq A^{k+1} k! M_k </math>
for all ''x''&nbsp;&isin;&nbsp;[''a'',''b''], some constant ''A'', and all non-negative integers ''k''. If ''M''<sub>''k''</sub>&nbsp;=&nbsp;1 this is exactly the class of real [[analytic function]]s on [''a'',''b'']. 

The class ''C''<sup>''M''</sup>([''a'',''b'']) is said to be ''quasi-analytic'' if whenever ''f''&nbsp;&isin;&nbsp;''C''<sup>''M''</sup>([''a'',''b'']) and
: <math>\frac{d^k f}{dx^k}(x) = 0</math>
for some point ''x''&nbsp;&isin;&nbsp;[''a'',''b''] and all ''k'', then ''f'' is identically equal to zero.

A function ''f'' is called a ''quasi-analytic function'' if ''f'' is in some quasi-analytic class.

=== Quasi-analytic functions of several variables ===

For a function <math>f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}</math> and multi-indexes <math>j=(j_1,j_2,\ldots,j_n)\in\mathbb{N}^n</math>, denote <math>|j|=j_1+j_2+\ldots+j_n</math>, and 
: <math>D^j=\frac{\partial^j}{\partial x_1^{j_1}\partial x_2^{j_2}\ldots\partial x_n^{j_n}}</math>
: <math>j!=j_1!j_2!\ldots j_n!</math>
and 
: <math>x^j=x_1^{j_1}x_2^{j_2}\ldots x_n^{j_n}.</math>

Then <math>f</math> is called quasi-analytic on the open set <math>U\subset\mathbb{R}^n</math> if for every compact <math>K\subset U</math> there is a constant <math>A</math> such that 
: <math>\left|D^jf(x)\right|\leq A^{|j|+1}j!M_{|j|}</math>
for all multi-indexes <math>j\in\mathbb{N}^n</math> and all points <math>x\in K</math>.

The Denjoy–Carleman class of functions of <math>n</math> variables with respect to the sequence <math>M</math> on the set <math>U</math> can be denoted <math>C_n^M(U)</math>, although other notations abound. 

The Denjoy–Carleman class <math>C_n^M(U)</math> is said to be quasi-analytic when the only function in it having all its partial derivatives equal to zero at a point is the function identically equal to zero.

A function of several variables is said to be quasi-analytic when it belongs to a quasi-analytic Denjoy–Carleman class.

=== Quasi-analytic classes with respect to logarithmically convex sequences ===

In the definitions above it is possible to assume that <math>M_1=1</math> and that the sequence <math>M_k</math> is non-decreasing. 

The sequence <math>M_k</math> is said to be ''logarithmically convex'', if 
: <math>M_{k+1}/M_k</math> is increasing.

When <math>M_k</math> is logarithmically convex, then <math>(M_k)^{1/k}</math> is increasing and 
: <math>M_rM_s\leq M_{r+s}</math> for all <math>(r,s)\in\mathbb{N}^2</math>.

The quasi-analytic class <math>C_n^M</math> with respect to a logarithmically convex sequence <math>M</math> satisfies:
* <math>C_n^M</math> is a ring. In particular it is closed under multiplication.
* <math>C_n^M</math> is closed under composition. Specifically, if <math>f=(f_1,f_2,\ldots f_p)\in (C_n^M)^p</math> and <math>g\in C_p^M</math>, then <math>g\circ f\in C_n^M</math>.

== Denjoy–Carleman theorem ==

The Denjoy–Carleman theorem, proved by {{harvtxt|Carleman|1926}} after {{harvtxt|Denjoy|1921}} gave some partial results,  gives criteria on the sequence ''M'' under which ''C''<sup>''M''</sup>([''a'',''b'']) is a quasi-analytic class. It states that the following conditions are equivalent: 
* ''C''<sup>''M''</sup>([''a'',''b'']) is quasi-analytic.
* <math>\sum 1/L_j = \infty</math> where <math>L_j= \inf_{k\ge j}(k\cdot M_k^{1/k})</math>.
* <math>\sum_j \frac{1}{j}(M_j^*)^{-1/j} = \infty</math>,  where ''M''<sub>''j''</sub><sup>*</sup> is the largest log convex sequence bounded above by ''M''<sub>''j''</sub>.
* <math>\sum_j\frac{M_{j-1}^*}{(j+1)M_j^*} = \infty.</math>

The proof that the last two conditions are equivalent to the second uses [[Carleman's inequality]].

Example: {{harvtxt|Denjoy|1921}} pointed out that if ''M''<sub>''n''</sub> is given by one of the sequences
: <math>1,\, {(\ln n)}^n,\, {(\ln n)}^n\,{(\ln \ln n)}^n,\, {(\ln n)}^n\,{(\ln \ln n)}^n\,{(\ln \ln \ln n)}^n, \dots,</math>
then the corresponding class is quasi-analytic. The first sequence gives analytic functions.

== Additional properties ==

For a logarithmically convex sequence <math>M</math> the following properties of the corresponding class of functions hold:
* <math>C^M</math> contains the analytic functions, and it is equal to it [[if and only if]] <math>\sup_{j\geq 1}(M_j)^{1/j}<\infty</math>
* If <math>N</math> is another logarithmically convex sequence, with <math>M_j\leq C^j N_j</math> for some constant <math>C</math>, then <math>C^M\subset C^N</math>.
* <math>C^M</math> is stable under differentiation if and only if <math>\sup_{j\geq 1}(M_{j+1}/M_j)^{1/j}<\infty</math>.
* For any infinitely [[differentiable function]] <math>f</math> there are quasi-analytic rings <math>C^M</math> and <math>C^N</math> and elements <math>g\in C^M</math>, and <math>h\in C^N</math>, such that <math>f=g+h</math>.

=== Weierstrass division ===

A function <math>g:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}</math> is said to be ''regular of order <math>d</math> with respect to <math>x_n</math>'' if <math>g(0,x_n)=h(x_n)x_n^d</math> and <math>h(0)\neq 0</math>. Given <math>g</math> regular of order <math>d</math> with respect to <math>x_n</math>, a ring <math>A_n</math> of real or complex functions of <math>n</math> variables is said to satisfy the ''Weierstrass division with respect to <math>g</math>'' if for every <math>f\in A_n</math> there is <math>q\in A</math>, and <math>h_1,h_2,\ldots,h_{d-1}\in A_{n-1}</math> such that 
: <math>f=gq+h</math> with <math>h(x',x_n)=\sum_{j=0}^{d-1}h_{j}(x')x_n^j</math>.

While the ring of analytic functions and the ring of formal [[power series]] both satisfy the Weierstrass division property, the same is not true for other quasi-analytic classes.

If <math>M</math> is logarithmically convex and <math>C^M</math> is not equal to the class of analytic function, then <math>C^M</math> does not satisfy the Weierstrass division property with respect to <math>g(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)=x_1+x_2^2</math>.
